title: Alan Turing and the Universal Machine (1936)
explainer: In 1936, Alan Turing described an abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape according to a fixed table of rules, and showed that one such machine could simulate any other — the first rigorous answer to the question of what can be computed at all. Every real computer, from a phone to a server, is a physical approximation of this same idea: a general-purpose machine that executes stored instructions rather than being hardwired for one task. Turing built the model to settle a problem in mathematical logic, not to build hardware, which is part of why the question 'what is a computer' has a cleaner answer in math than in engineering.

title: Von Neumann and the Stored-Program Computer (1945)
explainer: The basic shape of almost every computer today — one memory holding both instructions and data, fetched and executed one at a time by a control unit — comes from a 1945 report on the EDVAC machine usually attributed to John von Neumann. Historians note the underlying ideas were developed with engineers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, who had been working out the stored-program concept before von Neumann wrote the report, so 'von Neumann architecture' is really shorthand for a team effort. Knowing this origin explains why computers are built around a stored-program model rather than being rewired for every new task.
